question: While checking a twelve-page report, an analyst finds that one section has used last year's headcount figures. Which sequence should she follow next?
options: A) Correct that section; re-read the conclusions in light of the correction; look for the same error elsewhere; approve the report.
B) Look for the same error elsewhere; correct every affected section; re-read the conclusions in light of it; approve the report.
C) Re-read the conclusions in light of it; correct that section; approve the report; look for the same error elsewhere.
D) Approve the report; look for the same error elsewhere; correct every affected section; re-read the conclusions in light of it.
correct_answers: B) Look for the same error elsewhere; correct every affected section; re-read the conclusions in light of it; approve the report.
explanations: Fixing only the section where the error was noticed leaves identical errors elsewhere, and the conclusions are re-read before those are found.

Correct. One instance of stale data suggests a source problem rather than a typing slip, so the scope of the error is established first, every affected section is then corrected, and the conclusions are re-read against the corrected figures before approval.
Re-reading conclusions before the figures are corrected judges them against numbers already known to be wrong, and approval precedes the wider search.
Approval comes before any of the corrective work, so the report is signed off in the state that was already known to be wrong.
